faq.a: INR standardises PT across reagents, allowing reliable comparison and guiding warfarin therapy.
faq.q: Why is INR preferred to PT in most hospitals?

faq.a: Use PT/INR and clinical context; for suspected heparin effect, check anti‑Xa level if possible.

exam: A patient with severe malaria develops diffuse oozing from IV sites – which test will most likely be abnormal and why? — Expect prolonged PT/INR and aPTT due to consumptive coagulopathy (DIC).
You receive a lab report: INR 2.2, platelets 80 ×10⁹/L, normal aPTT. What is the next immediate step? — Give vitamin K and consider FFP if bleeding; investigate warfarin or liver disease.

A 30‑year‑old male on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with a head injury. Which coagulation test guides reversal and what is the target? — Check INR; aim for <1.5 before neurosurgical intervention, give vitamin K and FFP.

In a rural clinic without aPTT, a patient on unfractionated heparin shows a prolonged PT. How do you interpret this? — PT is not reliable for heparin; assess clinical bleeding and consider switching to low‑molecular‑weight heparin with anti‑Xa monitoring if available.

A postpartum woman has sudden vaginal bleeding, platelets 45 ×10⁹/L, PT 14 s, INR 1.2, aPTT 38 s. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Acute postpartum DIC; low platelets with relatively normal PT/INR suggest early consumptive phase.
Why is tranexamic acid contraindicated in patients with known DIC? — It blocks fibrinolysis, worsening microvascular thrombosis in DIC.
A child with hemophilia A presents with a prolonged aPTT but normal PT/INR. Which factor deficiency is most likely? — Factor VIII deficiency, characteristic of hemophilia A.
Explain how vitamin K deficiency affects PT more than aPTT. — Factor VII (extrinsic) has the shortest half‑life, so PT rises first; intrinsic factors decline later.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Coagulation tests help clinicians identify bleeding risk, monitor anticoagulation and detect liver‑related coagulopathy. In low‑resource hospitals, interpretation must consider test availability and common tropical conditions.

b: Prothrombin time (PT) assesses the extrinsic pathway and common factors (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen).
Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) assesses the intrinsic and common pathways (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogen).
Platelet count and bleeding time evaluate primary haemostasis.
sections.p: Coagulation tests measure the time for plasma to form a fibrin clot, reflecting the integrity of the extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways.

b: Mild: normal PT/INR (<1.3) and aPTT (<40 s) with isolated thrombocytopenia >100 ×10⁹/L.
Moderate: PT/INR 1.3‑1.8 or aPTT 40‑60 s, platelets 50‑100 ×10⁹/L, or minor mucosal bleeding.
Severe: PT/INR >1.8, aPTT >60 s, platelets <50 ×10⁹/L, or life‑threatening hemorrhage.
sections.p: Bleeding severity is staged by clinical impact and laboratory derangement rather than a formal numeric score.

b: Liver disease (viral hepatitis, schistosomiasis, alcohol) – prolonged PT/INR.
Vitamin K deficiency (poor diet, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, malabsorption) – prolonged PT, normal aPTT.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (sepsis, severe malaria, obstetric complications) – prolonged PT/aPTT, low platelets, high D‑dimer.
Anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, heparin) – isolated PT/INR or aPTT rise.
Inherited factor deficiencies (hemophilia A/B) – isolated aPTT prolongation.
sections.p: Identify whether the abnormality is due to reduced factor synthesis, consumption, inhibition or platelet dysfunction.

b: Petechiae or purpura suggest platelet or vascular problems.
Prolonged bleeding after minor cuts points to factor deficiency.
Bleeding from multiple sites (gums, IV sites) raises suspicion of DIC.
sections.p: Patients may present with spontaneous bruising, mucosal bleeding, postoperative oozing, or catastrophic hemorrhage.
Select tests that answer the clinical question; when a test is unavailable, use bedside clues or alternative assays.

t.b: Is the extrinsic pathway impaired? – Prolonged PT/INR indicates liver disease, vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect.
Is the intrinsic pathway impaired? – Prolonged aPTT suggests hemophilia, heparin effect or DIC.
Is primary haemostasis compromised? – Low count (<150 ×10⁹/L) explains mucosal bleeding and petechiae.
Is platelet function abnormal? – Prolonged bleeding time with normal count suggests uremia or antiplatelet drugs.
Is there consumptive coagulopathy? – High D‑dimer and low fibrinogen support DIC.
Is fibrinogen low or inhibited? – Prolonged TT indicates hypofibrinogenemia or heparin contamination.

b: INR >2.5 with active gastrointestinal bleed.
aPTT >80 s in a patient on heparin.
Platelets <20 ×10⁹/L with spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage.
sections.p: Uncontrolled bleeding can rapidly lead to hypovolemic shock and organ failure.

b: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) for rapid factor replacement when PT/INR >1.8 and bleeding.
Packed red cells for haemodynamic instability.
Tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic) for trauma‑related bleeding when fibrinolysis suspected.
Heparin reversal with protamine if aPTT excessively high.
Avoid NSAIDs and herbal anticoagulants in patients with abnormal tests.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, replace deficient components, and monitor response.

b: Check INR 24 h after vitamin K or FFP.
Monitor platelet trends in sepsis or malaria.
Educate patients on avoiding unsupervised herbal remedies that affect clotting.
sections.p: Repeat PT/INR and aPTT after interventions; screen high‑risk patients before surgery.

b: Thrombocytopenia vs. prolonged PT – platelet count low but PT normal in isolated platelet disease.
DIC vs. liver failure – both prolong PT/INR, but DIC shows low fibrinogen and high D‑dimer.
sections.p: Distinguish coagulation test abnormalities from platelet disorders and from primary fibrinolysis.

b: Heparin contamination can prolong aPTT in vitro; repeat sample without heparin.
Severe anemia may mask prolonged PT because of low plasma protein concentration.
Vitamin K antagonists may not affect PT if the assay reagent is insensitive; verify with INR.
sections.p: Certain conditions give falsely normal values.
